metadata.title: Claude, Mining.
metadata.subtitle: What's Actually in a Skill
metadata.purpose: Take apart the 'Claude skill' case: explain what Claude actually reads when it uses the mining skill, name the design choice (one short file, no code, no training) and what it buys, and name what it does not cover (anything the file doesn't say). Land the carry-out that a skill is Claude reading one short file, not Claude knowing more — so it can't answer past what that file says.

beats.narration_text: Here's what's actually happening. A Claude skill isn't Claude knowing more — it's Claude reading one short file right before it answers. They optimized for a scope you can audit in one glance. So what's actually inside that file?

beats.narration_text: A Claude skill is a folder Claude checks before it acts — that's the whole surface area. This one is called mining. Open the folder up, and there's exactly one file inside it: SKILL.md. No code, no config, no plugin — just a file Claude will read.

The reasonable-sounding read is that Claude already knows this — trained on years of Minecraft guides somewhere in the weights — and the skill is just permission to say so out loud. That is the guess this design has to defeat.

Open SKILL.md and it isn't permission, it isn't reasoning, it isn't a guide to cross-reference. It's one sentence: 'where diamonds spawn in Minecraft 1.20.' That is the entire file. They chose a scope you can audit at a glance over any cleverness Claude might bring from training. This is the anchor: the whole skill, on one line.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR — the whole file, one line

beats.narration_text: Claude reads that sentence and acts on it directly — no branching, no lookup, no extra reasoning invented along the way. Read the instruction, follow the instruction, hand back the answer. Linear on purpose: they optimized for a mechanism you can predict from the file alone, not one that improvises off it.

Ask twice, and you get the identical answer both times — that consistency is real, and it's what the design bought you. But ask about Minecraft 1.21 instead, or emeralds instead of diamonds, and there is nothing left to reach for. The file only ever said the one thing. This works if you value a predictable, auditable scope; it fails if you needed the skill to generalize past what's written.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR RETURNS — same sentence, both directions

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini: I want to understand what a Claude skill really is. Walk me through what Claude actually reads when it uses a skill, when it reads it, and what it does with the content — versus what it does not do. Then explain why a skill is one short file instead of code, a plugin, or fine-tuning: what does that choice buy, and what does it cost? Finally, design me a minimal SKILL.md for a skill called meeting-notes that turns a raw transcript into an action-items list; show the whole file and explain every line. Go deeper: ask the same model what happens when the SKILL.md instruction and Claude's training pull in different directions on a question the file only half-covers — which one wins, and how would you tell from the answer alone?
